newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. to end Yugoslav sanctions, keep assets frozen.
newsitem.headline: U.N. to end Yugoslav sanctions, keep assets frozen.

text.p: Europeans and the United States on Monday reached broad agreement on a resolution to end sanctions against Yugoslavia and expect the Security Council to approve it later this week.

Diplomats said a draft of the text drawn up by the contact group of major powers that coordinates policy on Yugoslavia was being sent to capitals overnight. Still to be decided was Germany's proposal to include a reference to the U.N. War Crimes Tribunal, while Russia wanted to stick to the sanctions issue.

Sanctions against the Yugoslav state, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, were suspended by the council last November as a followup to the U.S.-initiated Dayton peace accords. The council's resolution stipulated the sanctions would be lifted entirely 10 days after the Sept. 14 Bosnian elections. Russia had insisted that meant Sept. 24.

But Washington viewed the resolution as saying the elections first had to be certified by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which did so on Sunday despite charges of voting irregularities.
The draft resolution also said the council would be willing to consider reimposing sanctions should the Dayton accords be broken. But most envoys believe Russia would block such a move in the future.

However the document will not release Belgrade's frozen assets because of disputes and claims from successor states, such as Croatia, Bosnia, Slovenia and Macedonia, after the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, the envoys said.
Also held in abeyance will be Yugslavia's re-admittance to the U.N. General Assembly and other bodies in the world organisation from which it was suspended because of its disputed legal status.

The United States said previously it would keep a so-called outer ring of sanctions, such as preventing the rump Yugoslav state of Serbia and Montenegro from institutions like the International Monetary Fund.

Britain's Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind agreed and said last week that western European states have linked Yugoslavia's re-entry to financial institutions to progress on the restive Serbian province of Kosovo, dominated by ethnic Albanians.

The contact group at the United Nations includes Britain, France, Russia, Germany, Italy as well as the United States. All six had agreed at a meeting among their ministers last week to terminate the sanctions as soon as certification arrived.

In Washington, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the sanctions would be "formally lifted I think just in a matter of days. The United States will support this because it meets the criteria that we helped to negotiate at Dayton."

He said the certification, coupled with the first meeting of Moslem, Serb and Croat members of the Bosnian presidency, meant the peace process was moving forward and the sanctions could be terminated.
